title: Having a strong grip won't give you big forearms
summary: NH debunks the idea that a strong (static crush) grip from deadlifting builds big forearms. Forearm size depends heavily on muscle insertions; static holds are the least hypertrophic stimulus; grip strength depends on hand size and the nervous system. Forearm growth needs progressive overload across wrist and elbow flexions and all grip types, isolation work, and possibly arm-wrestling training.

claims.claim: There are many types of grip (crush, pinch, static, dynamic, wrist and elbow flexion); the powerlifting-centric static crush grip is only one and probably the least important for forearm hypertrophy.
Crush grip strength gives some forearm growth, but it doesn't keep rising with the weight you deadlift.
For every natural powerlifter with big forearms you can find ten who pull the same weight with small forearms.
Forearm size depends largely on muscle insertions: the higher the muscle belly inserts, the bigger the forearm looks and the more growth potential it has.
People who got big forearms just from pulls likely have gifted insertions and would have had them anyway.
Telling people to just deadlift more to grow forearms is idiotic; grip eventually becomes the limit, and the gripped weight is neither challenging for the back nor enough for the forearms.
Static holds sit at the bottom for forearm hypertrophy: an isometric stretch, a way almost no other muscle is trained.
Full range of motion, as heavy as you can go, grows muscle best; for forearms that means wrist flexions and elbow flexions.
Static grip strength is most influenced by hand size and finger length, since fingers provide leverage on the bar.
Basing forearm training on grip misleads both big-handed people (strong grip, small forearms) and small-handed people (weak grip, think they are cursed); both need forearm isolation work.
There are people with 600 lb deadlifts from the floor who don't have big forearms.
NH says his outer forearms are nothing special but his inner forearms are pretty big.
Pro bodybuilders with 16-17 inch forearms often don't have particularly strong grips; grip depends on hand size and nervous-system strength.
Anecdote: a man with stick forearms could tear a deck of cards with his fingers, while a 30-year construction worker with massive forearms could not.
Apply progressive overload to every area of grip and forearm function, not just static holds; static holds are good for the front of the forearm because of the stretch.
Try arm-wrestling training: arm wrestlers have massive forearms because they train the forearm in a flexed position under load.
Using straps actually helps forearm growth (topic of a follow-up video).

exercises.name: Static holds
exercises.why: least hypertrophic, but good stretch for front of forearm
